title: How to Win Friends and Influence People
author: Dale Carnegie
tagline: Thirty timeless principles for handling people, being liked, persuading and leading.

superpower.name: People Magnet
superpower.description: People like you and want to help you.

overview: Carnegie's classic is organised as practical principles in four parts: fundamental techniques for handling people, six ways to make people like you, twelve ways to win people to your way of thinking, and nine ways to change people without giving offence. Each module below covers one principle.

chapters.part: Fundamental Techniques in Handling People
chapters.title: Don't criticise, condemn or complain
chapters.summary: Criticism makes people defensive and rarely changes behaviour; it wounds pride and breeds resentment. Most people, even wrongdoers, justify themselves. Instead of condemning, try to understand why people do what they do — it creates sympathy, tolerance and kindness.
keyIdeas: Seek to understand instead of condemn.
chapters.tryThis: Go a full day without criticising anyone.

quiz.question: Why does Carnegie say criticism is futile?
options: It makes people defensive and resentful
quiz.explanation: Defensive people justify themselves rather than change.

chapters.part: Fundamental Techniques in Handling People
chapters.title: Give honest and sincere appreciation
chapters.summary: One of the deepest human desires is to feel important. Sincere appreciation meets that need, while flattery — insincere praise — is quickly seen through. Look for people's genuine strengths and acknowledge them generously.
chapters.tryThis: Give three people specific, sincere appreciation today.

quiz.question: What separates appreciation from flattery?
quiz.explanation: Appreciation is honest; flattery is not.

chapters.part: Fundamental Techniques in Handling People
chapters.title: Arouse in the other person an eager want
chapters.summary: People care about what they want, not what you want. To influence someone, talk about their desires and show how to get them. Seeing things from their angle — as well as your own — is the key to persuasion.
keyIdeas: See from their point of view.
chapters.tryThis: Before a request, write down what the other person gains from saying yes.

quiz.question: What's the key to motivating others here?
quiz.explanation: Connect your request to their desires.

chapters.part: Six Ways to Make People Like You
chapters.title: Become genuinely interested in other people
chapters.summary: You make more friends by being interested in others than by trying to get them interested in you. Ask about their lives, remember details and show you care. Genuine interest is magnetic.
chapters.tryThis: Ask someone a follow-up question about something they mentioned last time.

quiz.question: How do you make friends fastest?
quiz.explanation: Interest in others draws them to you.

chapters.part: Six Ways to Make People Like You
chapters.title: Smile
chapters.summary: A sincere smile says 'I like you, you make me happy, I'm glad to see you.' It costs nothing and creates goodwill instantly — even over the phone it changes your voice. Acting cheerful can help you feel cheerful.
chapters.tryThis: Smile at everyone you greet today and notice the responses.

quiz.question: What does a sincere smile communicate?
quiz.explanation: It shows warmth and goodwill.

chapters.part: Six Ways to Make People Like You
chapters.title: Remember names
chapters.summary: A person's name is, to them, the sweetest sound. Remembering and using it makes people feel valued; forgetting it can feel like a slight. Make the effort: repeat it, associate it and use it.
chapters.tryThis: Use the name of each new person you meet at least twice in conversation.

quiz.question: Why remember names?
quiz.explanation: A name signals that you see the person.

chapters.part: Six Ways to Make People Like You
chapters.title: Be a good listener
chapters.summary: People are far more interested in themselves than in you. Encourage them to talk about themselves and listen attentively. Many people known as great conversationalists simply listened well.
keyIdeas: Encourage others to talk about themselves.
chapters.tryThis: In your next chat, speak less than a third of the time.

quiz.question: What makes someone a 'good conversationalist' per Carnegie?
quiz.explanation: People love those who listen to them.

chapters.part: Six Ways to Make People Like You
chapters.title: Talk in terms of the other person's interests
chapters.summary: The royal road to someone's heart is to talk about what they treasure most. Research their interests before you meet and steer conversation there; both of you benefit from the connection.
keyIdeas: Find out what others care about.
chapters.tryThis: Before meeting someone, learn one thing they're passionate about.

quiz.question: What topic wins people over?
quiz.explanation: People warm to talk of what they love.

chapters.part: Six Ways to Make People Like You
chapters.title: Make the other person feel important — sincerely
chapters.summary: Everyone wants to feel important. Treat people as if they matter, because they do: show respect, thank them, and acknowledge their contributions. Small courtesies go a long way.
chapters.tryThis: Thank someone for a specific contribution they rarely get credit for.

quiz.question: What must accompany making others feel important?
quiz.explanation: Insincere attention backfires.

chapters.part: How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking
chapters.title: The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it
chapters.summary: Even if you win an argument, you lose the person's goodwill. Arguments usually entrench both sides. Welcome disagreement, control your temper, look for areas of agreement and thank people for their interest.
keyIdeas: You can't truly win an argument.
chapters.tryThis: In a disagreement, start by naming what you agree on.

quiz.question: What's the best way to win an argument?
quiz.explanation: Winning an argument still loses goodwill.

chapters.part: How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking
chapters.title: Show respect for others' opinions; never say 'You're wrong'
chapters.summary: Telling someone they're wrong attacks their intelligence and pride, making them dig in. Instead say 'I may be wrong — let's examine the facts.' Diplomacy keeps minds open.
keyIdeas: Allow that you may be wrong.
chapters.tryThis: Replace 'You're wrong' with 'I may be wrong, let's check.'

quiz.question: What phrase does Carnegie suggest instead of 'You're wrong'?
quiz.explanation: It invites joint examination instead of defence.

chapters.part: How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking
chapters.title: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
chapters.summary: Admitting a mistake before others point it out disarms criticism and often wins generosity. Saying the critical things about yourself first leaves others little to attack — and earns respect.
chapters.tryThis: Own one small mistake out loud before anyone mentions it.

quiz.question: What happens when you admit fault quickly?
quiz.explanation: It removes the need for others to criticise.

chapters.part: How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking
chapters.title: Begin in a friendly way
chapters.summary: A drop of honey catches more flies than a gallon of gall. Starting friendly lowers defences and makes people more willing to be persuaded than starting with demands or anger.
chapters.tryThis: Open your next difficult conversation with a genuine kind word.

quiz.question: Why begin in a friendly way?
quiz.explanation: Friendliness opens minds.

chapters.part: How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking
chapters.title: Get the other person saying 'yes, yes' immediately
chapters.summary: Begin with points you agree on so the other person says 'yes' early. Each yes builds momentum toward agreement, while an early 'no' makes people defend their position.
keyIdeas: An early no is hard to reverse.
chapters.tryThis: Ask two questions you know they'll agree with before making your point.

quiz.question: Why aim for early 'yes' responses?
quiz.explanation: Agreement breeds agreement.

chapters.part: How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking
chapters.title: Let the other person do a great deal of the talking
chapters.summary: People persuade themselves best. Let them talk through their ideas and concerns; you'll learn what matters to them and they'll feel heard. Resist the urge to interrupt.
chapters.tryThis: Ask an open question and let silence work before you respond.

quiz.question: What's the benefit of letting others talk?
options: They feel heard and you learn their concerns
quiz.explanation: Listening uncovers what will persuade them.

chapters.part: How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking
chapters.title: Let the other person feel the idea is theirs
chapters.summary: People value ideas they discover themselves. Make suggestions, ask questions and let others reach the conclusion. You give up credit but gain commitment.
chapters.tryThis: Ask 'What do you think we should do?' instead of giving the answer.

quiz.question: Why let people feel an idea is theirs?
options: They commit more to their own ideas
quiz.explanation: Self-discovered ideas get followed through.

chapters.part: How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking
chapters.title: Try honestly to see things from the other person's point of view
chapters.summary: People rarely do things without a reason that makes sense to them. Ask yourself how you'd feel in their place; understanding their view reduces conflict and makes your case more relevant.
chapters.tryThis: Write down how the other side sees a current disagreement.

quiz.question: What does seeing their view do?
quiz.explanation: Understanding lets you address what matters to them.

chapters.part: How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking
chapters.title: Be sympathetic with the other person's ideas and desires
chapters.summary: Saying 'I don't blame you for feeling that way; I'd feel the same' can defuse hostility. People hunger for sympathy, and offering it calms tempers and opens the way to cooperation.
chapters.tryThis: When someone is upset, acknowledge their feelings before solving anything.

quiz.question: What does sympathy do in a tense moment?
quiz.explanation: Acknowledged people calm down.

chapters.part: How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking
chapters.title: Appeal to the nobler motives
chapters.summary: People usually have a good-sounding reason and a real reason for what they do. Appealing to their nobler motives — fairness, honesty, honour — encourages them to live up to them.
keyIdeas: People like to see themselves as good.
chapters.tryThis: Frame a request around fairness rather than pressure.

quiz.question: Which motives should you appeal to?
quiz.explanation: People rise to the image you appeal to.

chapters.part: How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking
chapters.title: Dramatize your ideas
chapters.summary: Facts alone rarely persuade. Showmanship — vivid demonstrations, stories and visuals — makes ideas memorable and convincing. Stage your point so people feel it.
chapters.tryThis: Turn your next pitch's key point into a quick demonstration or story.

quiz.question: Why dramatize ideas?
quiz.explanation: People remember what they experience.

chapters.part: How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking
chapters.title: Throw down a challenge
chapters.summary: People are motivated by the desire to excel and to prove their worth. A friendly competition or challenge can spark effort that orders and money cannot.
chapters.tryThis: Set a team a friendly target with recognition for beating it.

quiz.question: What does a challenge tap into?
quiz.explanation: Competition brings out effort.

chapters.part: Be a Leader
chapters.title: Begin with praise and honest appreciation
chapters.summary: Like a barber who lathers before shaving, start feedback with genuine praise. It makes the harder message easier to hear without feeling attacked.
chapters.tryThis: Start your next piece of feedback with a genuine strength.

quiz.question: How should feedback begin?
quiz.explanation: It opens the door to listening.

chapters.part: Be a Leader
chapters.title: Call attention to people's mistakes indirectly
chapters.summary: Pointing out mistakes directly often causes resentment. Indirect hints, and replacing 'but' with 'and' after praise, let people correct themselves without losing face.
chapters.tryThis: Rephrase 'Good job, but…' as 'Good job, and next time…'.

quiz.question: Which word should replace 'but' after praise?
quiz.explanation: 'And' keeps the praise intact.

chapters.part: Be a Leader
chapters.title: Talk about your own mistakes before criticising
chapters.summary: Admitting your own errors first makes criticism easier to accept. It shows humility and signals that mistakes are part of learning.
chapters.tryThis: Mention a similar mistake you once made before correcting someone.

quiz.question: Why mention your own mistakes first?
options: It makes criticism easier to accept
quiz.explanation: Shared fallibility builds trust.

chapters.part: Be a Leader
chapters.title: Ask questions instead of giving direct orders
chapters.summary: Questions like 'What do you think of this?' or 'Could we try…?' preserve dignity and invite cooperation. People are more willing to act on decisions they helped shape.
chapters.tryThis: Turn one instruction today into a question.

quiz.question: What do questions do that orders don't?
quiz.explanation: People cooperate when they're consulted.

chapters.part: Be a Leader
chapters.title: Let the other person save face
chapters.summary: Even when someone is clearly wrong, humiliating them destroys goodwill. Give people a dignified way out; protecting their pride protects the relationship.
chapters.tryThis: Correct someone privately instead of in front of others.

quiz.question: What does letting someone save face protect?
quiz.explanation: Humiliation creates lasting resentment.

chapters.part: Be a Leader
chapters.title: Praise every improvement
chapters.summary: Praise even the slightest improvement, specifically and sincerely. Recognition encourages people to keep improving, while criticism tends to shut them down.
chapters.tryThis: Notice and praise one small improvement in someone today.

quiz.question: What should you praise?
quiz.explanation: Small praise encourages continued growth.

chapters.part: Be a Leader
chapters.title: Give the other person a fine reputation to live up to
chapters.summary: People tend to live up to the reputation you give them. Assume the best and say so; showing confidence in someone's qualities often brings those qualities out.
keyIdeas: People rise to a good reputation.
chapters.tryThis: Tell someone a strength you see in them that you want them to use.

quiz.question: What happens when you give someone a fine reputation?
options: They try to live up to it
quiz.explanation: People rise to expectations.

chapters.part: Be a Leader
chapters.title: Use encouragement; make faults seem easy to correct
chapters.summary: If a skill seems hard, people give up. Encourage them, express faith in their ability and make the fault seem easy to fix, and they'll practise until they improve.
chapters.tryThis: Tell someone struggling that the fix is small and they can do it.

quiz.question: Why make faults seem easy to correct?
options: People keep trying when success seems possible
quiz.explanation: Belief in success drives practice.

chapters.part: Be a Leader
chapters.title: Make the other person happy about doing what you suggest
chapters.summary: Effective leaders make people glad to do what they ask by being sincere, focusing on benefits to the other person, and matching the request to their interests and talents.
chapters.tryThis: When delegating, explain what the person will gain or enjoy.

quiz.question: What makes people happy to follow a suggestion?
quiz.explanation: People act willingly when it serves them too.
